meta.description: No Marx work contains this line. Wikiquote lists it as Disputed; the earliest occurrence yet located is a 1952 Communist Review article, not Marx.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Democracy is the road to socialism'?
meta.ogDescription: Marx is not the source. Wikiquote rates it Disputed, earliest known print use 1952. Here is what Marx actually wrote about democracy.

answer.label: Not traced to Marx — an unsourced 20th-century slogan
answer.authorDates: 1818–1883 · German philosopher, political theorist & revolutionary socialist
answer.sourceLine: No book, article, letter or speech by Marx has been shown to contain this sentence, and Wikiquote files it under “Disputed” ↗, noting that the earliest occurrence yet located is The Communist Review (Communist Party of Great Britain, 1952), p. 15, where it is used to characterise the Communist agenda rather than quoted from Marx. The thought has a real Marxian pedigree — the Communist Manifesto calls winning “the battle of democracy” the first step of the workers’ revolution — but this six-word slogan is a later compression, not Marx’s wording.
answer.confidenceText: No Marx source — Wikiquote rates it Disputed

source.heading: What Marx actually wrote

docMeta.dd: None on record — no work, letter or speech contains this sentence
The Communist Review (Communist Party of Great Britain, 1952), p. 15
Manifesto of the Communist Party (1848), ch. 2 · trans. Samuel Moore with Frederick Engels, 1888

source.excerpt: We have seen above, that the first step in the revolution by the working class is to raise the proletariat to the position of ruling class, to win the battle of democracy.
trail: Wikiquote’s Karl Marx page ↗ places the line in its Disputed section — not “Misattributed” — and states that the earliest occurrence yet located is The Communist Review (1952) by the Communist Party of Great Britain, p. 15, where it characterises the Communist agenda. It names Tom Lansford’s Communism (2007), p. 48 as an example of the recent attribution to Marx.

The nearest thing Marx genuinely wrote is in chapter 2 of the Communist Manifesto ↗: the first step of the workers’ revolution is “to win the battle of democracy.” That is a step in a programme, not the slogan.

Marx made the point again in “The Chartists,” New-York Daily Tribune, 25 August 1852 ↗, arguing that carrying universal suffrage in England “would, therefore, be a far more socialistic measure than anything which has been honored with that name on the Continent. Its inevitable result, here, is the political supremacy of the working class.”
The quote circulates today with no citation attached. Goodreads ↗ credits it to Marx with no book or source line, under its own notice that quotes are added by the community and are not verified.
source.excerptNote: This is not the quote. It is the closest thing Marx actually wrote — from chapter 2 of the Communist Manifesto ↗, in the standard English translation by Samuel Moore with Frederick Engels (1888). Marx frames democracy as the workers’ first step, not as a “road” leading anywhere by itself.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because the sentence has no identified author or work. It is not traceable to Marx, and the earliest use yet located — a 1952 issue of The Communist Review — is both post-1931 and not a Marx text, so nothing here supports a public-domain claim for this wording. Marx’s own 1848 Manifesto in the 1888 Samuel Moore translation quoted above is long out of copyright, but that is a different sentence.

author.name: Karl Marx
author.heading: About Karl Marx
author.metaLine: 1818–1883 · German philosopher, political theorist & revolutionary socialist
author.bio: Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia in 1818, Marx spent most of his working life in exile, settling in London after the failed revolutions of 1848. With Friedrich Engels he wrote the Manifesto of the Communist Party that year, and he spent his later decades on Das Kapital, his critique of political economy. He was also a working journalist — his New-York Daily Tribune columns of the 1850s are where much of his most direct writing on democracy and the vote appears. He died in London in 1883, and the sheer volume of what he actually wrote is part of why unsourced one-liners attach to him so easily.

misattribution.heading: How Marx got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a slogan in search of an author. It reads like Marx, it summarises something Marx broadly argued, and it is short enough to fit a placard — which is most of what a quotation needs to acquire a famous name. What it has never had is a citation.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under Disputed and says it has been “attributed to Marx in recent years,” while the earliest occurrence yet located dates from 1952 — long after Marx’s death in 1883. No Marx work has been produced that contains it.

items.who: The Communist Review, Communist Party of Great Britain
items.why: In the earliest use Wikiquote could find — The Communist Review (1952), p. 15 — the sentence is “used to characterize the Communist agenda” ↗, that is, as a description of communist strategy rather than as words quoted from Marx. It is worth noting that the CPGB had published its parliamentary-strategy programme The British Road to Socialism ↗ the previous year, in 1951 — it was retitled Britain’s Road to Socialism only with the seventh edition in 2001; the resemblance in phrasing is an observation, not a documented derivation.

Wikiquote names this reference book, at p. 48 ↗, as an instance of the line being attributed to Marx in print. A published book repeating an attribution is how an unsourced slogan acquires the appearance of a source.

items.who: Goodreads, AZQuotes and similar quote sites
items.why: AZQuotes ↗ presents the line under Marx’s name with topic tags and no work, date or citation of any kind, and Goodreads ↗ does the same beneath a notice that its quotes are community-submitted and unverified.

misattribution.truthLine: Marx did argue that democracy was the workers’ route to power — “to win the battle of democracy” ↗ is his own phrase, from the Communist Manifesto. But “Democracy is the road to socialism” is not a sentence he is known to have written, and the version that spread came from somewhere else.

context.heading: Why this one travels
lead: The slogan works because it is doing political labour for two opposed camps at once. Read approvingly, it is a communist party’s case for contesting elections rather than storming palaces. Read as a warning, it is proof that voting is a trapdoor. The same six words serve both readings, which is exactly why nobody circulating them has much incentive to go looking for a citation.

Marx’s real position was more specific and more conditional than the slogan. In 1852 he argued that universal suffrage in England would be genuinely revolutionary because of the particular class arithmetic there — the proletariat formed the large majority, and the countryside had no peasantry left, only landlords, capitalist farmers and hired labourers. That is an argument about one country’s conditions, not a general law that democracy leads to socialism everywhere.
detailsBody: The 1952 date matters. By the early 1950s the question of whether socialism could arrive through parliament was the live strategic argument inside European communist parties, and the Communist Party of Great Britain had just published The British Road to Socialism (1951) — retitled Britain’s Road to Socialism only in 2001 — a programme built on winning a parliamentary majority pledged to socialism. A phrase of this shape belongs naturally to that mid-century debate rather than to Marx’s own century.

None of which proves Marx never wrote something like it — proving a negative across an enormous body of journalism, correspondence and manuscripts is not possible. What can be said is what the record shows: no located source in Marx, an earliest known appearance in 1952, and a modern circulation that carries no citation at all.
context.pull: A slogan that serves two opposed camps equally well is a slogan nobody has an interest in checking.

schema.verdictNote: Widely credited to Karl Marx, but no work, letter or speech of Marx’s has been shown to contain it; Wikiquote files the line under Disputed rather than Misattributed. The true author is not established; no creator is asserted here.
schema.claimRatingName: Disputed — no source in Marx located

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Democracy is the road to socialism" in its Disputed section for Karl Marx, states it was attributed to Marx in recent years including in Communism (2007) by Tom Lansford, p. 48, and that the earliest occurrence yet located is The Communist Review (1952) by the Communist Party of Great Britain, p. 15, where it is used to characterize the Communist agenda.

The Communist Manifesto, chapter 2, contains: "We have seen above, that the first step in the revolution by the working class is to raise the proletariat to the position of ruling class, to win the battle of democracy."

The Marxists Internet Archive edition of the Communist Manifesto states the English text was "Translated: Samuel Moore in cooperation with Frederick Engels, 1888" and that it was first published February 1848.

Marx's article "The Chartists" (New-York Daily Tribune, Vol. 12 No. 3543, 25 August 1852) states that carrying universal suffrage in England "would, therefore, be a far more socialistic measure than anything which has been honored with that name on the Continent. Its inevitable result, here, is the political supremacy of the working class."

Goodreads presents "Democracy is the road to Socialism" attributed to Karl Marx with no source, book or citation, under a notice that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.

AZQuotes presents "Democracy is the road to socialism." credited to Karl Marx with only topic tags (Socialism, Democracy, Liberty, Historical, Libertarian, Libertarianism) and no work, date or citation.

The Internet Archive holds Tom Lansford's book Communism (creator: Lansford, Tom; publisher: New York, Marshall Cavendish Benchmark), the reference work Wikiquote cites as attributing the line to Marx at p. 48.

The programme was first published in 1951 by the Communist Party of Great Britain as The British Road to Socialism, advocating a parliamentary road to socialism using existing democratic rights to achieve a parliamentary majority pledged to socialism; it was retitled Britain's Road to Socialism with the seventh edition in 2001.

Wikipedia's "Democratic road to socialism" article covers the theory associated with Nicos Poulantzas and notes the argument (Tristram Hunt, Bruno Jossa) that Marx and Engels grew skeptical of top-down revolutions in their later writings in favour of a peaceful, democratic road to socialism.
Karl Marx was born 5 May 1818 in Trier, Kingdom of Prussia, died 14 March 1883, and is described as a German philosopher, social and political theorist, and revolutionary socialist.
